clinicalPearls: Hyperbaric oxygen therapy (HBO2T) means breathing physician-prescribed medical-grade oxygen while the whole body is enclosed in a chamber pressurized to at least 2.0 ATA; most regimens use 2-2.8 ATA for roughly 90-120 minutes per session.

At 2.8 ATA, arterial Po2 can theoretically rise above ~2025 mmHg and dissolved plasma oxygen to ~60 mL/L, enough to sustain life without hemoglobin in animal studies, which sharply improves oxygen diffusion through tissues.

Even a single HBO2T exposure produces durable cell-signaling effects (on fibroblasts, leukocytes, angiogenesis, antioxidant defenses) that persist for hours after oxygen levels return to baseline, mediated by reactive oxygen and nitrogen species.

The UHMS recognizes 15 accepted indications, including air/gas embolism, carbon monoxide poisoning, gas gangrene, crush injury, decompression sickness, problem wounds, intracranial abscess, necrotizing soft tissue infection, refractory osteomyelitis, delayed radiation injury, and sudden sensorineural hearing loss.

For chronic problem wounds, candidate selection is often guided by transcutaneous oximetry around the wound while breathing air and oxygen at pressure; in diabetic patients a transcutaneous Po2 threshold of <50 mmHg may be more appropriate than the usual <40 mmHg cutoff.

Carbon monoxide binds hemoglobin with more than 200 times the affinity of oxygen and shifts the oxyhemoglobin dissociation curve leftward; HBO2T shortens the COHb half-life to about 21 min at 2.0 ATA versus roughly 5.5 h breathing air at sea level.
Admission carboxyhemoglobin levels confirm CO exposure but do NOT reliably predict severity or prognosis; delayed neuropsychological sequelae can appear after days to months of apparent recovery.
Ambient pressure increases by 1 atmosphere (101.3 kPa) for every 10.1 m of seawater, so a diver at 20 m experiences about 3 ATA.

In diving, the maximum acceptable inspired Po2 is generally considered 1.6 ATA (lower than therapeutic HBO2T pressures) because immersion and exercise raise the risk of oxygen-toxic seizures; helium replaces nitrogen at depth to cut narcosis and gas density.

Cerebral arterial gas embolism (CAGE) from pulmonary barotrauma presents within minutes of surfacing with loss of consciousness, confusion, hemiplegia, visual or speech disturbance, and can be mistaken for stroke or TIA by clinicians unfamiliar with diving.

Decompression sickness occurs in roughly 1 in 5000-10,000 recreational dives; most cases are mild (limb pain, fatigue, patchy paresthesias), and serious DCS usually appears within 60 min of surfacing.
Symptoms beginning more than 24 h after a dive are very unlikely to be DCS unless the diver was subsequently exposed to reduced ambient pressure such as air travel or higher-altitude surface travel.

About 25% of adults have a patent foramen ovale; right-to-left shunting (PFO, atrial septal defect, intrapulmonary shunt) lets venous bubbles 'arterialize' and raises the risk of cerebral, spinal cord, inner ear, and skin DCS manifestations.
harrison.pathophysiology: Hyperbaric oxygen exerts effects through both physical mechanisms and biochemical cell signaling. Physically, raising ambient pressure shrinks gas bubbles per Boyle's law and steepens inert-gas diffusion gradients from bubble to tissue to blood and lungs, the basis for treating decompression sickness and arterial gas embolism. The markedly elevated arterial Po2 fully saturates hemoglobin and greatly increases dissolved plasma oxygen, improving diffusion into hypoxic and irradiated tissue. Beyond simple oxygen delivery, intermittent hyperoxia generates reactive oxygen species (superoxide, hydrogen peroxide) and reactive nitrogen species (nitric oxide) that drive cytokine and angiogenic growth-factor production, stimulate fibroblast activity, enhance macrophage bacterial killing, mobilize vasculogenic progenitor cells from marrow, and paradoxically produce anti-inflammatory effects such as reduced leukocyte beta-2 integrin adhesion. Hyperoxia also causes vasoconstriction and an osmotic gradient that reduce tissue edema and is directly toxic or bacteriostatic to anaerobes. In late radiation tissue injury, irradiation produces fibrosis and obliterative endarteritis leaving hypovascular hypoxic tissue (an alternative model emphasizes cytokine-driven fibrosis from oxidative stress and mitochondrial dysfunction); HBO2T's most important benefit is promoting angiogenesis and increasing microvascular density. In carbon monoxide poisoning, CO impairs oxygen carriage, acts as an anesthetic, disrupts cellular oxidative processes, binds heme proteins including cytochrome a/a3, and peroxidizes brain lipids, with brain and heart most vulnerable. In diving, breathing gas at elevated ambient pressure loads inert gas (usually nitrogen) into tissues; if washout during ascent lags the falling ambient pressure, tissues become supersaturated and bubbles form, causing mechanical distortion of tissues and, in the venous circulation, inflammatory and coagulation cascades, endothelial injury, capillary leak, hemoconcentration, and pulmonary vascular obstruction. Barotrauma arises when noncompliant gas-filled spaces fail to equalize with changing ambient pressure.
additionalDifferentials: Stroke or transient ischemic attack (can mimic or be mimicked by cerebral arterial gas embolism)
Inner ear barotrauma versus vestibulocochlear decompression sickness (both cause sensorineural hearing loss and vertigo)
Middle ear barotrauma (should never be invoked to explain post-dive sensorineural hearing loss or true vertigo)
Acute coronary syndrome or musculoskeletal injury versus DCS limb pain
Other causes of post-dive neurologic symptoms not explained by an alternative mechanism
nonInfectiousMimics: Migraine or other transient neurologic events after diving
Decompression sickness mimicking CAGE and vice versa (clinically the distinction is unimportant because first aid and definitive management are identical)
additionalInvestigations: Transcutaneous oximetry (transcutaneous Po2 mapping) around a wound on air and on oxygen at pressure to assess HBO2T suitability
Ankle-brachial index and skin perfusion pressure as alternative wound perfusion assessments
Carboxyhemoglobin level in suspected CO poisoning (confirms exposure but does not gauge severity or prognosis)
Arterial blood-gas analysis for metabolic acidosis in CO poisoning (a marker of poor prognosis)
Audiometry / otologic evaluation for suspected inner ear barotrauma
Dive profile review combined with clinical examination (there are no useful confirmatory diagnostic tests for DCS)
redFlags: Neurologic symptoms after diving (loss of consciousness, confusion, hemiplegia, visual or speech disturbance) suggesting CAGE or serious DCS — discuss with a diving medicine specialist and consider recompression
Spinal cord involvement in DCS (weakness, paralysis, bladder/sphincter dysfunction) which frequently causes permanent disability
Pulmonary and cardiovascular DCS manifestations (cough, dyspnea, hypotension, hemoconcentration, coagulopathy) which can be life-threatening
Sensorineural hearing loss or true vertigo with nausea, vomiting, nystagmus, ataxia after diving (inner ear barotrauma or vestibulocochlear DCS)
Untreated pneumothorax before any hyperbaric exposure (intrapleural gas can expand and tension on decompression)
Tonic-clonic seizure during HBO2T or diving from cerebral oxygen toxicity, sometimes preceded by facial twitching, anxiety, and agitation
Moderate-to-severe CO poisoning, especially age over 35, prolonged exposure, acidosis, or loss of consciousness
harrison.prognosis: Most HBO2T adverse events are mild and self-limiting, and the therapy is generally safe. For late radiation tissue injury pooled data suggest improved tissue healing and reduced wound dehiscence in jaw osteoradionecrosis. About 70% of indolent problem ulcers are substantially improved or healed 6 months after a course, and meta-analyses report increased complete healing and reduced amputation of diabetic foot ulcers. In CO poisoning the most rigorous trial showed fewer cognitive sequelae at 6 weeks (25% vs 46%) and 12 months (18% vs 32%) with HBO2T, though a Cochrane review found overall evidence insufficient. Survivors of CO poisoning may develop delayed neuropsychological sequelae; risk factors for poor outcome are age over 35, exposure beyond 24 h, acidosis, and loss of consciousness. In diving, CAGE often shows substantial or complete early resolution as bubbles involute, but secondary deterioration or re-embolization can occur. Most DCS cases are mild, but spinal cord DCS frequently causes permanent disability and pulmonary/cardiovascular forms can be fatal.
pitfalls: Attributing post-dive sensorineural hearing loss or true vertigo to middle ear barotrauma — these point instead to inner ear barotrauma or vestibulocochlear DCS.
Misdiagnosing CAGE as a typical stroke or TIA when the clinician is unfamiliar with diving medicine.
Relying on admission carboxyhemoglobin level to judge severity or prognosis of CO poisoning.
Assuming there is a confirmatory diagnostic test for DCS — diagnosis rests on dive profile, symptom timing, and examination.
Treating CAGE/DCS distinction as clinically critical — first aid and definitive management are the same for both.
Compressing a patient with an untreated pneumothorax or with gas-trapping lesions such as bullae without careful risk assessment and, for pneumothorax, a patent chest drain.

Overstating the risk of pulmonary oxygen toxicity from remote bleomycin exposure; published experience suggests the relationship may have been exaggerated, though recent bleomycin or mitomycin C with pneumonitis warrants careful evaluation.
Promoting HBO2T (sometimes with air) as a panacea for unproven indications, general well-being, or anti-aging — practice should be confined to accepted, periodically updated indications.
harrison.severityClassification: Decompression sickness manifestations (Harrison Table 476-2) are grouped by organ system: musculoskeletal (limb pain); neurologic cerebral (confusion, visual and speech disturbances), spinal (weakness, paralysis, upper motor neuron signs, bladder/sphincter dysfunction, dermatomal sensory disturbance, abdominal/girdle pain), vestibulocochlear (hearing loss, vertigo, ataxia, nausea/vomiting), and peripheral (patchy nondermatomal sensory disturbance); pulmonary (cough, dyspnea); cardiovascular (hemoconcentration, coagulopathy, hypotension); cutaneous (rash, itch); lymphatic (localized soft tissue edema); and constitutional (fatigue, malaise). Most cases are mild; serious DCS usually manifests within 60 min of surfacing.
management: Treat decompression sickness and arterial gas embolism with recompression and hyperbaric oxygen, preceded by high-flow surface oxygen and horizontal positioning during transfer

Provide adjunctive intravenous fluid resuscitation and analgesia for decompression illness, and definitive care for the specific injury such as debridement and antibiotics for necrotising soft-tissue infection or gas gangrene

Deliver hyperbaric oxygen for its accepted indications including carbon monoxide poisoning, crush injury, refractory osteomyelitis, delayed radiation tissue injury and problem wounds, following recognised protocols
Select chronic problem-wound candidates using transcutaneous oximetry around the wound while breathing air and oxygen at pressure
Screen for and manage barotrauma before and during treatment, equalising middle-ear pressure and watching for pulmonary and sinus barotrauma
Monitor for central-nervous-system and pulmonary oxygen toxicity and confinement-related complications during sessions
Refer to a dive or hyperbaric medicine physician for dive-profile review and coordinated multidisciplinary management
